header.title_plain: Fasted cardio burns more fat during the session — and doesn't change how much fat you lose
header.evidence_type: Narrative review aimed at physique athletes, drawing on two meta-analyses of acute effects, one meta-analysis of body-composition outcomes (5 studies, 96 people), and a handful of trials.

confidence.why: The "no difference" finding rests on meta-analyses; the physique-athlete caveats are the authors' speculation.

practical_relevance.why: Directly answers one of the most common "I saw it online" questions.

header.author_stance: one author is a physique coach (stated); no conflicts declared
header.funding_and_conflicts: No funding; no conflicts (one author is a physique coach).

review.claim: Fasted aerobic exercise does raise fat oxidation during the session and has some favourable acute effects. But controlled studies find trivial-to-no difference in fat loss between fasted and fed cardio when calories are matched. Physique athletes at very low body fat haven't been studied, so small advantages can't be ruled out. Protein before cardio may be the best of both.

evidence_cited.finding: Fasted exercise burns more fat during the session
evidence_cited.numbers: 27 studies, 273 participants; low-intensity (~40–70% HRmax); blood glucose not different (p = 0.91)

evidence_cited.finding: Fasted training raises stored muscle glycogen
evidence_cited.numbers: +22% basal muscle glycogen in fasted group; no change fed

evidence_cited.finding: Fasted exercise uses fat stored inside muscle
evidence_cited.numbers: intramuscular triglyceride ↓ ~60% fasted; no change fed

evidence_cited.finding: More fatty acids circulate when fasted
evidence_cited.numbers: 46 studies; FFA higher fasted; other markers mixed and population-dependent
19 active men, 3×/wk, 40–60 min at 60–80% HRmax. Weight: fasted 79.2→77.7 kg, fed 80.5→78.4 kg (both sig). Body fat: fasted 19.4→18.6% (sig), fed 19.3→18.8% (not sig).
evidence_cited.note: But fed group ate 3,056 vs 2,466 kcal/day (calorie confound); skinfold measurement.

evidence_cited.numbers: 5 studies, 96 participants (60 M, 36 F), age 21–27: trivial-to-small effects on weight, % fat, lean mass
20 women, 4 weeks, hypocaloric diet, 1.8 g/kg protein, 60 min walking 3×/wk supervised. Fasted: 26.3→25.0% fat, 16.5→15.4 kg fat. Fed: 24.8→24.1%, 15.7→15.0 kg.
nitrogen loss ≈ 14 g amino acids/h during 60 min fasted exercise
greater post-exercise energy expenditure fed vs fasted

11 men, crossover: 25 g whey / casein / maltodextrin / nothing, then 30 min at 55–60% HR reserve. Protein → higher post-exercise energy expenditure and fat oxidation; casein > whey during exercise; fasting did not raise fat oxidation

recommendations_made: Protein before cardio is the authors' own practical pick: it may protect muscle, slightly raises post-exercise burn, and doesn't blunt fat use the way carbohydrate does.
Avoid fasted sessions longer than 60 minutes because of protein loss.
review.untested_or_contested: No studies in physique competitors (lean, high-protein, resistance-trained, 8–16+ week preps). Small effects below statistical significance might matter at the margin of competition. Thermogenic supplements commonly taken before fasted cardio may change the picture.

layer2.what_it_means: Burning more fat during a workout and losing more fat overall are different things, and the evidence separates them cleanly. Fasted cardio shifts fuel use for an hour; over weeks, the body balances it out, and fat loss tracks the calorie deficit. So the honest answer to "should I do fasted cardio?" is: if you like it and it helps you be consistent, fine; if you hate it, you're giving up nothing by eating first. The authors' own practical pick is protein before cardio — it may protect muscle, slightly raises post-exercise burn, and doesn't blunt fat use the way carbohydrate does. They also advise against fasted sessions longer than 60 minutes because of protein loss.
layer2.what_it_doesnt_mean: It doesn't prove fasted cardio is useless — it proves it's not better in the populations studied, who were mostly untrained, overweight, or young women on short trials. The authors hold open a door for very lean competitors, but that's a hypothesis they're explicit about. And none of this is about fasted lifting, high-intensity work, or intermittent fasting as a diet.

translation: Fasted vs fed cardio, matched calories, 4 weeks: ~1.1 kg vs ~0.7 kg fat lost, not a significant difference.
Fasted: more fat burned in the session; fed: more burned afterwards. Net: about the same.
If fasted: keep it under 60 min and low-to-moderate intensity. Or have 25 g protein first.

glossary_candidates.definition: Aerobic exercise done after an overnight fast, before eating.
Fat oxidation is fat burned right now; fat loss is the change in body fat over time, which depends on total energy balance.
Fat stored inside muscle fibres; a fuel for moderate exercise, especially when fasted.
A study that pools the results of many studies to get a more reliable overall answer.
How big a difference is, independent of whether it's statistically significant; "trivial" means too small to matter.
Calories in minus calories out; fat loss over time requires a sustained deficit.
Cardio done after a protein-only feed (e.g. 25 g whey or casein).
